traveler: Simon bar Jonah, called Cephas, the Apostle Peter
title: The Nets to the Inverted Cross: Simon of Bethsaida, the Rock, and the Road to Rome
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Bethsaida, the fisherman's town
stops.date_confidence: Hometown attested at John 1:44, which names Bethsaida as the town of Andrew, Peter, and Philip. The date is a placeholder for the years before the calling and rests on nothing. Which mound is Bethsaida is an open archaeological dispute: el-Araj, pinned here, has produced a Byzantine church and a 2022 mosaic inscription invoking Peter as chief and commander of the heavenly apostles, while et-Tell (32.9103, 35.6306) remains the older rival candidate.
stops.campa: Simon son of John is born at Bethsaida on the north shore of the lake, in a house that lives by nets. His brother Andrew works beside him. The town sits where the Jordan comes down into the water, close enough to Capernaum that a man can move his boat and his household the few miles west without changing his trade. He learns the wind on that water, the seasons of the sardine and the tilapia, the mending of linen mesh by lamplight. Nothing in the record says he learns to read.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bethsaida', on the el-Araj and et-Tell excavations
suggested_refs: The el-Araj excavation and its 2022 mosaic inscription naming Peter
The rival mound of et-Tell, north of the lake

stops.name: Bethany beyond the Jordan, Andrew brings his brother
stops.date_confidence: John 1:35-42 places the naming here, at the Baptist's station on the Jordan, at first meeting. Matthew 16:17-19 places it years later at Caesarea Philippi, tied to the confession. The two Gospels do not agree on when or where the byname was given, and this file does not harmonize them: both stops stand. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Andrew has been standing with John the Baptist at the river when the Baptist points and says, Behold the Lamb of God. He follows, stays the day, and then goes to find his brother: We have found the Messiah. He brings Simon down to the water. Jesus looks at him, and before Simon has said anything at all, gives him a name: You are Simon son of John. You are to be called Cephas. No one on record has carried that word as a name before. It is Aramaic. It means a stone.
stops.quote: You are Simon son of John. You are to be called Cephas (which is translated Peter).
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bethany beyond the Jordan' (Al-Maghtas), for the site
suggested_refs: The baptism site at Al-Maghtas, east bank of the Jordan

stops.name: The shore near Capernaum, the nets left in the water
stops.date_confidence: Mark 1:16-20, generally taken as the earliest Gospel, followed closely by Matthew 4:18-22. Luke 5 and John 1 give incompatible settings and sequences for the same calling; the divergence is flagged here and not resolved. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He is casting a net into the lake with Andrew when the teacher from Nazareth comes along the shore and says, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of people. They leave the net in the water. A little further on, the sons of Zebedee are in the boat mending gear, and James and John leave their father with the hired men and do the same. Mark takes five verses over the whole thing and gives no reason why any of them go. Four fishermen, two pairs of brothers, one morning's work left floating.
suggested_refs: The basalt shoreline between Capernaum and Tabgha

stops.name: The lake of Gennesaret, the catch that breaks the nets
stops.date_confidence: Luke 5:1-11 relocates the calling entirely: Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, orders a catch, and Simon kneels in it. This is a second and incompatible calling tradition alongside Mark 1:16-20. The consecutive dates order the file and assert no reconciliation between the two accounts.
stops.campa: The crowd presses to the water's edge, so Jesus gets into Simon's boat, asks him to put out a little from the land, and teaches sitting down from the stern. When he has finished he tells Simon to go into the deep water and let down the nets. Simon says they have worked all night and taken nothing, and lets them down anyway. The catch nearly swamps two boats. Simon goes down on his knees among the fish and asks him to go away, because he is a sinful man.
suggested_refs: The first-century Galilee boat recovered at Ginosar in 1986

stops.name: Capernaum, the fever leaves his wife's mother
stops.date_confidence: Mark 1:29-31, with Matthew 8:14-15 and Luke 4:38-39. The marriage is independently corroborated by Paul at 1 Corinthians 9:5, written decades before the Gospels reached final form. The excavated house being Simon's own is the excavators' inference, not certain. Coordinates are the Capernaum pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Out of the synagogue they go straight to the house Simon shares with Andrew, where Simon's wife's mother is lying with a fever. Jesus takes her hand and lifts her, and the fever leaves, and she gets up and serves them. By sundown the whole town is at the door with its sick. The house is a courtyard dwelling of black basalt a stone's throw from the water; within a lifetime its main room will be replastered and given over to gathering, and in the fifth century an octagonal church will be built so that its floor sits exactly over these walls.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Capernaum', on the Franciscan excavation of the House of Peter
suggested_refs: The fifth-century octagonal church over the house at Capernaum
The 1990 memorial church built on stilts with a glass floor above the ruins

stops.name: The open water, walking out to him
stops.date_confidence: Matthew 14:22-33 alone carries Peter's walk on the water. Mark 6:45-52 and John 6:16-21 narrate the same crossing without it. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The boat is far from land in the fourth watch, battered by waves and a headwind, when they see him walking on the sea and cry out that it is a ghost. Peter says, Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water. Come, says Jesus. He goes over the side. For a few steps the water holds him. Then he notices the wind, and starts to go down, and shouts, Lord, save me. A hand closes on his. You of little faith, why did you doubt? They climb back in and the wind drops.
suggested_refs: The open water between Tabgha and the eastern shore

stops.name: Caesarea Philippi, the confession and the keys
stops.date_confidence: Matthew 16:16-19 for the keys and for binding and loosing; Mark 8:29-30 records the confession without them and Luke 9:20 abbreviates further. The keys saying is Matthew's alone, which matters for every later claim built on it. Coordinates are the Banias pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: At the springs under Hermon, beside the great rock face and the cut niches of Pan, in the town Philip named for Caesar and for himself, Jesus asks who people say he is, and then who they say he is. Simon answers for all of them: You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. Mark, telling the same scene, records the confession and nothing after it. In Matthew the reply gives Simon the name a second time and hangs a weight on it: rock, church, gates of Hades, keys, binding and loosing.
stops.quote: Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you but my Father in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of Pan and the spring cave at Banias
Perugino, Delivery of the Keys, Sistine Chapel, 1481-82, which puts this saying on a wall

stops.name: Mount Tabor, the light and the three shelters
stops.date_confidence: Matthew 17:1-8 and parallels name only a high mountain. The identification with Tabor is Origen's, third century, and became the pilgrimage standard, though nineteenth-century scholars objected that a fortified town stood on the summit in the first century. Coordinates are the Mount Tabor pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Six days after the confession he takes Peter, James, and John up the mountain by themselves, the three he takes everywhere the others do not go: to Jairus's bedside, up here, later into the deep part of the garden. His face changes and his clothes turn white, and Moses and Elijah stand there talking with him. Peter, who does not know what to say, says something anyway, about building three shelters. A cloud comes over them while he is still speaking, and a voice out of it, and they go down on their faces.
sources: Mark 5:37 and 14:33 (NRSVUE) for the inner three
Wikipedia, 'Mount Tabor', on the disputed identification
suggested_refs: The Church of the Transfiguration on the summit of Tabor

stops.name: The Cenacle, the feet he does not want washed
stops.date_confidence: John 13:1-11 for the footwashing and 13:36-38 for the prediction of the denial. The location on Mount Zion is a later pilgrimage identification and is not fixed by the text. Coordinates are the Cenacle pin already in use in this corpus. The day follows the Passion chronology conventionally and is not independently dated.
stops.campa: At the supper Jesus gets up, ties a towel round himself, and begins washing the disciples' feet. When he reaches Peter, Peter pulls back: You will never wash my feet. He is told that unless he is washed he has no share in what is coming, and he swings the whole way over at once, in the way he has, asking for his hands and his head as well. Later at the same table he is told that before the cock crows he will three times deny knowing the man who is speaking to him. He answers that he will die first.
suggested_refs: The upper hall on Mount Zion, over the traditional tomb of David

stops.name: Gethsemane, the sword and the servant's ear
stops.date_confidence: Mark 14:32-42 for the watch, John 18:10-11 for the sword. All four Gospels report the blow; only John names Peter as the man who struck it and only John names the slave Malchus. The divergence is recorded and not resolved. Coordinates are the Gethsemane pin already in use in this corpus.
stops.campa: Among the olives he is told to stay awake and cannot; three times Jesus comes back and finds the three of them asleep. Then the torches come up the slope with Judas at the head of them. Peter has a sword. He draws it and swings at the high priest's slave and takes off the man's right ear, and the slave's name, which John alone preserves, is Malchus. Luke alone adds that Jesus touches the ear and heals it. Put your sword back into its sheath, he is told, and he puts it back.
suggested_refs: The rock of the Agony under the Church of All Nations

stops.name: The courtyard of the high priest, the cock crowing
stops.date_confidence: Mark 14:66-72 with parallels at Matthew 26, Luke 22, and John 18. The four accounts agree on the triple denial and diverge on the identity of the questioners and the staging. The site on Mount Zion is traditional, attested from the fourth-century Bordeaux Pilgrim's itinerary of the house of the priest Caiaphas near this spot. Coordinates are the Gallicantu pin already in use in this corpus.
stops.campa: He follows at a distance, the whole way into the courtyard, and sits down among the guards at the fire to see how it ends. A servant girl studies him in the firelight and says he was with the Nazarene. He says he does not know what she is talking about. She says it again to the bystanders and he denies it again. An hour on they tell him his Galilean accent gives him away, and he begins to curse and to swear. Then the cock crows and he remembers and goes outside and weeps.
stops.quote: I do not know this man you are talking about.
suggested_refs: The Byzantine and Crusader remains under St Peter in Gallicantu
The Bordeaux Pilgrim's itinerary of 333, naming the house of Caiaphas

stops.name: The tomb, the linen wrappings lying there
stops.date_confidence: Luke 24:12 and John 20:3-10. The event is attested in two Gospels. The identification of the tomb with the site under the Church of the Holy Sepulchre is a later tradition, not fixed by the texts. Coordinates are the empty-tomb pin already in use in this corpus.
stops.campa: The women come back saying the stone is rolled away, and the eleven take it for an idle tale. Peter runs anyway. In John he is outrun by the other disciple, who stoops at the opening and looks in and waits there, and Peter comes up behind him and goes straight inside, which is the order these two keep falling into. The linen wrappings are lying on the shelf and the cloth that was on the head is rolled up by itself in its own place. He goes home wondering what has happened.
suggested_refs: The aedicula over the traditional tomb in the Anastasis rotunda

stops.name: Jerusalem, he appeared to Cephas
stops.date_confidence: 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, a creedal formula Paul says he received and relayed in the mid-50s, decades earlier than any Gospel reached final form. This is the earliest surviving claim of a resurrection appearance to Peter. Paul gives no location; the Jerusalem placement is inferred from the parallel at Luke 24:34 and is not fixed by the text. Coordinates are the Jerusalem pin already in use in this corpus. The day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Before there is a Gospel, before anyone has written a line of narrative, there is a formula the believers say to each other, which Paul later sets down as something handed to him and not invented: that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. The name stands first in the list. Luke keeps the same order in a single line the disciples shout to the pair from Emmaus.
stops.quote: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
suggested_refs: The pre-Pauline creedal formula of 1 Corinthians 15:3-5

stops.name: Tabgha, the charcoal fire and the three questions
stops.date_confidence: John 21:1-19, undated within the text beyond being after the resurrection. The Mensa Christi rock and the church on the shore are later devotional identifications; the appearance itself is textual. Coordinates are the Galilee restoration pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He has gone back to the boats. I am going fishing, he tells them, and they fish all night and take nothing. At first light a man on the beach tells them to try the other side, and the net comes up so heavy they cannot haul it aboard. Peter puts his clothes on to swim ashore. There is a charcoal fire burning on the stones, with bread, and fish already on it. Three times he is asked whether he loves him. Three times he says yes. Three times he is told to feed the sheep. The third time it hurts, and he says so.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Church of the Primacy of St. Peter', for the Mensa Christi
suggested_refs: The Mensa Christi limestone outcrop at Tabgha

stops.name: Jerusalem, the lot that falls on Matthias
stops.date_confidence: Acts 1:15-26, Luke's composition. The historical core is plausible; the speech is not a transcript and there is no external corroboration. Coordinates are the Jerusalem pin already in use in this corpus. The day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: About a hundred and twenty of them are gathered when Peter stands up in the middle of the room and says that the scripture had to be fulfilled, and that Judas's place must be filled by a man who was with them the whole way, from the baptism of John to the day their teacher was taken up, so that he can stand as a witness to the resurrection with the rest of them. Two names go forward, Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. They pray, and cast lots, and the lot falls on Matthias, who is numbered with the eleven.
suggested_refs: The upper room of Acts 1, traditionally the Cenacle on Mount Zion

stops.name: The Temple Mount, the morning of Pentecost
stops.date_confidence: Acts 2:14-41. The speeches in Acts are Luke's compositions and may preserve earlier tradition without being transcripts; the crowd figure of three thousand is Luke's and is uncorroborated. Coordinates are the Temple Mount pin already in use in this corpus. The day is a placeholder within the festival.
stops.campa: The noise brings a crowd, and the crowd decides the men are drunk. Peter stands up with the eleven and raises his voice: these men are not drunk, it is nine in the morning. He gives them Joel on the last days and the spirit poured out on all flesh, then David on the one who would not be abandoned to Hades, then the accusation without any softening, that they crucified the man God has made both Lord and Messiah. They ask what they should do. Repent, he says, and be baptized, every one of you.
suggested_refs: The southern steps and the mikva'ot at the Huldah Gates, Temple Mount

stops.name: Solomon's Portico, the lame man and the council
stops.date_confidence: Acts 3:1-4:22 for the healing and the first hearing, Acts 5:17-42 for the second arrest and the flogging. Acts-only narrative with no external corroboration, though the Sanhedrin's policing role is documented elsewhere. Coordinates are the Temple Mount pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: A man lame from birth is carried up daily to the Beautiful Gate to beg from the people going in. Peter tells him there is no silver and no gold, and takes him by the right hand, and the man goes into the Temple walking and leaping. The crowd runs after them to Solomon's Portico and Peter preaches there until the priests and the captain of the Temple arrest him. The council cannot deny the healing and orders him to stop using the name. He asks them to judge whether he should obey them or God.
suggested_refs: The eastern colonnade of the Temple platform, called Solomon's Portico

stops.name: Jerusalem, the price kept back
stops.date_confidence: Acts 5:1-11, an Acts-only episode with no external record. Acts frames the two deaths as divine judgment and does not present Peter as carrying out an execution. Coordinates are the Jerusalem pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The community is selling property and laying the proceeds at the apostles' feet. Ananias sells a field, keeps back part of the price with his wife's knowledge, and brings the rest. Peter asks him why Satan has filled his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit, and tells him the land was his own and the money was his own; he has lied not to men but to God. Ananias falls down and dies, and the young men wrap him and carry him out. Three hours later his wife comes in, not knowing, and is asked whether the price was the whole price.
suggested_refs: The common purse of Acts 4:32-37, the practice the episode polices

stops.name: Sebaste, the man who offered money for the Spirit
stops.date_confidence: Acts 8:14-24 for the episode, which is attested to Acts. Acts does not name which Samaritan city; the identification with Sebaste is conventional and is R. The later apocryphal expansion, in which Simon and Peter contest in Rome, has no support here. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Philip has been preaching in Samaria and baptizing, and Peter and John go down so that the Spirit will come on those already baptized. A magician named Simon, whom the whole city has followed and called the power of God that is called great, watches the hands laid on and offers them money for the ability. Peter tells him his silver can perish with him, that he has no part or share in this, that his heart is not right before God, and tells him to repent and pray. Simon answers by asking them to pray for him instead, that none of it comes on him.
sources: Eusebius, Church History 2.13-14, for the later Roman expansion of the story
suggested_refs: The Roman-era ruins of Sebaste at Sebastia
The word simony, formed from this transaction

stops.name: Jerusalem, fifteen days in Cephas's house
stops.date_confidence: Galatians 1:18-19, Paul's own firsthand testimony and the earliest independent evidence that Peter was a known, visitable figure in Jerusalem. Paul gives no address. The date rests on Paul's after three years counted from his own call, which is itself not independently dated. Coordinates are the Jerusalem pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: A man who held the coats at Stephen's stoning, and then went house to house in Judea hunting believers, arrives in the city three years after the road to Damascus and stays fifteen days under Peter's roof. Paul writes it down himself, decades later, in the middle of an argument about where his own authority came from: he went up to visit Cephas, he stayed fifteen days, and of the other apostles he saw only James the Lord's brother. What passed between them in those fifteen days neither man records.
stops.quote: Then after three years I did go up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and stayed with him fifteen days.
sources: Acts 9:26-30 (NRSVUE), which tells the visit differently
suggested_refs: Paul's autobiographical section, Galatians 1:11-2:14

stops.name: Lydda, the man on the mat for eight years
stops.date_confidence: Acts 9:32-35, an Acts-only episode with no external corroboration. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Going here and there among the believers, Peter comes down to the saints at Lydda on the plain of Sharon, a day's walk inland from the sea on the road that runs from Jerusalem to the coast. He finds a man there named Aeneas, bedridden and paralyzed for eight years. Jesus Christ heals you, he says. Get up and make your bed. Luke, the only writer who records the visit at all, has everyone living in Lydda and the Sharon turn to the Lord on the strength of it. The man gets up and makes his bed.
suggested_refs: The Church of St George at Lod, over the traditional site of the town's early community

stops.name: Joppa, the sheet let down by four corners
stops.date_confidence: Acts 9:36-43 and 10:9-16 for the episodes, which are attested to Acts. The seafront building shown today as the house of Simon the Tanner is a much later devotional identification and is R; it could not be confirmed archaeologically. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: They send for him from Joppa because Tabitha is dead, the woman who made tunics for the widows. He puts them all out of the upper room, kneels, and says, Tabitha, get up. Afterward he stays in the port many days with a tanner named Simon, in a house by the sea, a trade that keeps a man at the edge of a town and at the edge of ritual cleanness. On the roof at noon, hungry, he sees a sheet let down by its four corners with every kind of animal in it, and a voice telling him to kill and eat. Three times he refuses.
suggested_refs: The house shown at Jaffa as Simon the Tanner's, a devotional identification

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the household of the centurion
stops.date_confidence: Acts 10:1-48. The vision and the speeches are Luke's theological narration. Paul independently confirms at Galatians 2:12 that Peter did eat with gentiles before the Antioch dispute, which corroborates the underlying practice without the vision's specifics. Coordinates are the Caesarea Maritima pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Cornelius is a centurion of the Italian Cohort in the Roman provincial capital, a gentile who prays and gives alms, and his men are already at the gate in Joppa while Peter is still on the roof puzzling over the sheet. He goes with them, thirty miles up the coast, walks into a house full of gentiles, and says out loud that it is unlawful for a man like him to be standing there. God has shown me not to call anyone profane. While he is still speaking the Spirit falls on everyone listening, and he asks who can withhold the water.
suggested_refs: The Roman harbor and praetorium of Caesarea Maritima

stops.name: Jerusalem, answering for the water
stops.date_confidence: Acts 11:1-18, continuing directly from the Cornelius episode; Luke's narrative, uncorroborated externally. Coordinates are the Jerusalem pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Word gets to Judea before he does: Peter has gone into the house of uncircumcised men and eaten with them. When he arrives the believers of the circumcision take him to task, and he answers by telling the whole thing over in order, the sheet, the voice, the three refusals, the six brothers who came with him, the Spirit falling on gentiles exactly as it fell at the beginning. If God gave them the same gift, who was I to hinder God? They are silenced, and Luke closes the scene there, with the objection dropped and nothing decided in writing.
suggested_refs: The circumcision party of Acts 11:2, the same faction named at Galatians 2:12

stops.name: Jerusalem, the chains fall off in Herod's prison
stops.date_confidence: Acts 12:1-17. Acts ties the arrest to the Passover immediately preceding the death of Herod Agrippa I, which Josephus dates independently at Antiquities 19.343-350 to 44 CE; the research pool's 42 was inconsistent with that anchor and is corrected here to 44. The escape is Acts-only and its framing is miraculous. The day is a placeholder within the festival.
stops.campa: Agrippa has already had James son of Zebedee killed with the sword, and it pleased the people, so he takes Peter too and holds him under four squads of soldiers through the days of Unleavened Bread, meaning to produce him after the Passover. On the last night he is asleep between two soldiers, bound with two chains. A light fills the cell, a hand strikes his side, the chains drop off his wrists. He thinks he is seeing a vision until he is standing alone in the street. Then he departs for another place, and Acts does not say where.
sources: Josephus, Antiquities 19.343-350, for the death of Agrippa I in 44 CE
suggested_refs: The house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where Rhoda leaves him at the gate

stops.name: Jerusalem, the right hand of fellowship
stops.date_confidence: Galatians 2:1-10, Paul's own firsthand account. Whether this meeting is the same one Acts 15 narrates, reshaped by Luke, or a different meeting altogether, is disputed among scholars and is left open here rather than harmonized. Coordinates are the Jerusalem pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Paul comes up with Barnabas and Titus and lays out in private the gospel he has been preaching among the gentiles, in case he has been running for nothing. James, Cephas, and John, whom Paul calls the acknowledged pillars, give him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship and divide the work between them: Paul to the uncircumcised, Peter to the circumcised. The man who had walked into a Roman centurion's house and baptized the household takes the mission to the Jews. They ask one further thing, that the poor be remembered.
suggested_refs: The pillars formula of Galatians 2:9, James, Cephas, and John in that order

stops.name: Antioch, opposed to his face
stops.date_confidence: Galatians 2:11-14, Paul's firsthand account and the single strongest contemporary evidence of conflict involving Peter. Paul records neither Peter's reply nor the outcome; the episode is never resolved in the surviving text. Coordinates are the Antioch on the Orontes pin already in use in this corpus; the Cave Church of St Peter on Mount Starius stands at 36.2094, 36.1783. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: In Antioch, where the believers were first called Christians, Peter eats with the gentile members of the community as a matter of course. Then men arrive from James, and he draws back and separates himself, and the other Jewish believers follow him out, Barnabas included. Paul confronts him in front of everyone. The charge is not doctrine but inconsistency: if you, though a Jew, live like a gentile, how can you compel gentiles to live like Jews? Paul sets the scene down years later and stops at his own last word.
stops.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face because he stood self-condemned, for until certain people came from James, he used to eat with the gentiles. But after they came, he drew back and kept himself separate for fear of the circumcision faction.
sources: Acts 11:26 (NRSVUE), for the naming of Christians at Antioch
suggested_refs: The Cave Church of St Peter on Mount Starius above Antakya
The Feast of the Chair of Peter at Antioch, 22 February

stops.name: Jerusalem, the yoke on the neck
stops.date_confidence: Acts 15:6-21. Whether Luke is narrating the same meeting Paul reports at Galatians 2, or a separate one, is unresolved; the two accounts are not harmonized here. The speech is Luke's composition. Coordinates are the Jerusalem pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The question is whether gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul, writing his own account of these years, mentions no ruling and no list. Acts has Peter stand up after long debate and argue from his own experience at Caesarea: God made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith, so why put a yoke on their necks that neither our ancestors nor we have been able to carry. James then delivers the ruling. Gentiles are to abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality.
suggested_refs: The apostolic decree of Acts 15:19-20 and its four abstentions

stops.name: Corinth, I belong to Cephas
stops.date_confidence: 1 Corinthians 1:12 for the faction and 9:5 for the wife, both attested and both written from Ephesus in the mid-50s. That Peter personally visited Corinth is R, asserted only around 170 by Dionysius of Corinth in a letter preserved by Eusebius. The pin marks the church that quarreled over his name, not an attested visit. Coordinates are the Corinth pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Paul writes to the Corinthians that each of them is saying I belong to Paul, or I belong to Apollos, or I belong to Cephas, or I belong to Christ, and asks whether Christ has been divided. There is a Cephas party in a Greek port twenty-five years after the lake, and no evidence that the man himself has ever walked in the place. In the same letter, defending his right to be fed, Paul asks whether he alone lacks the right to travel with a believing wife, as the other apostles do, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas.
sources: Dionysius of Corinth, in Eusebius, Church History 2.25
suggested_refs: The bema at ancient Corinth
Dionysius of Corinth's letter to Rome, c. 170, claiming Peter planted the Corinthian church

stops.name: Rome, the arrival nobody can date
stops.date_confidence: R. Eusebius, Church History 2.13-14 places Peter's coming to Rome in the reign of Claudius, 41-54, and gives no year; the precise second year of Claudius comes from Eusebius's Chronicle, followed by Jerome, and the research pool's 44 from Church History is corrected to that. Against the tradition stands Romans 16, written before Paul had ever been in the city, which greets many people by name and not Peter. Ignatius, To the Romans 4, is the earliest indirect witness to a Petrine association with Rome.
stops.campa: The tradition says he comes to the capital under Claudius, that Simon the magician has gone ahead of him and is being honored there, and that the magician's power is quenched once Peter preaches in the city. No letter of Peter's or Paul's says plainly that Peter was ever in Rome. Paul writes to the Roman church before he has seen it, greets twenty-six people there by name, and does not greet Peter. Ignatius, on his way to die in the arena sixty years later, tells the Romans he does not command them as Peter and Paul did.
stops.quote: I do not, as Peter and Paul, issue commandments unto you. They were apostles; I am but a condemned man: they were free, while I am, even until now, a servant.
stops.quote_source: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Romans 4, tr. Roberts-Donaldson
sources: Eusebius, Chronicle, and Jerome, for the second year of Claudius
suggested_refs: Justin Martyr's report of a Roman statue he took for Simon Magus, quoted by Eusebius
The Liber Pontificalis and Jerome, On Illustrious Men, on a twenty-five-year Roman episcopate

stops.name: Rome, Mark writes the preaching down
stops.date_confidence: R. Eusebius, Church History 2.15, drawing on Papias at 3.39. Eusebius supplies no year, only the Claudian context carried over from 2.14, so this date is an ordering device and nothing more; the pool's 45 is not sourced. Clement's and Eusebius's versions differ on whether Peter approved the work or was indifferent to it. Mark is conventionally dated c. 65-75, decades after the tradition's own setting, a tension the tradition does not address.
stops.campa: His hearers in the city are not content to have heard him once. They press Mark, who has followed him and remembers what he said, to leave them a written monument of the teaching they were given by mouth, and they keep asking until he does it. Clement has Peter approve the finished work; Eusebius elsewhere has him take no interest in it either way. What comes of it is the shortest of the Gospels, the one that runs at a breathless pace and does not spare Peter: rebuked as Satan, asleep in the garden, denying with curses at the fire.
sources: Papias, quoted at Eusebius, Church History 3.39
suggested_refs: Papias on Mark as Peter's interpreter, the whole basis of the tradition

stops.name: Rome, his wife led away
stops.date_confidence: R. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 7.11, preserved at Eusebius, Church History 3.30, under the heading of the apostles who were married. Eusebius gives no date and no place for the wife's death and preserves no name for her; the research pool's 60 is invented and is dropped. The date here orders the segment and the Rome pin follows the surrounding martyrdom cluster only. That Peter had a wife who traveled with him is attested at 1 Corinthians 9:5.
stops.campa: The story Clement of Alexandria hands on is a few words long in the part that matters. Peter sees his own wife led away to be killed. Eusebius copies the passage down a century later and files it under the apostles who were married, giving no place for it and no year, and preserving no name for her. What Clement does preserve is that Peter called out to her by name, glad that she had been called and was going home, encouraging her and comforting her: Remember the Lord.
stops.quote_source: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 7.11, preserved at Eusebius, Church History 3.30
suggested_refs: Eusebius, Church History 3.30, The Apostles that were Married

stops.name: The Tullianum, water in the floor of the prison
stops.date_confidence: R throughout. No first-century record connects Peter to the Mamertine, and the Catholic Encyclopedia itself notes that the spring in the chamber long predates any Christian prisoner and that there is little firsthand account of an imprisonment here. Coordinates are the Mamertine pin already in use in this corpus. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Below the Capitoline, under the old Comitium, there is a round chamber of tufa with a hole in its floor, where Rome kept the condemned in the days before it killed them. The tradition puts Peter and Paul in it at the end. In the story a spring rises in the stone at Peter's word so that he can baptize the two guards who have charge of him, Processus and Martinian, and they are executed for it afterward. The spring in that floor is older than the story by centuries, and the church that owns it says so in its own guidebooks.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mamertine Prison', citing the Catholic Encyclopedia's own skepticism
suggested_refs: The Tullianum below San Giuseppe dei Falegnami, Clivo Argentario

stops.name: The Appian Way, Domine quo vadis
stops.date_confidence: R. The scene comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter, chapter 35, composed c. 150-200; there is no first-century support of any kind. The church of Santa Maria in Palmis on the spot was rebuilt in 1637 over a site venerated since at least the ninth century and shows a copy of a footprint stone, the original being kept at San Sebastiano fuori le mura. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The persecution is on and the brothers talk him into saving himself, so he goes out through the gate alone at night. On the Appian Way, a mile out among the tombs, he meets the Lord walking the other way, toward the city. Lord, where are you going? I am going to Rome to be crucified again. Peter turns around and walks back the way he came. In the floor of the little church later built on the spot there is a marble slab with two footprints cut into it, pointing toward Rome.
stops.quote: Lord, whither goest thou thus (or here)?
stops.quote_source: Acts of Peter, ch. 35, tr. M. R. James
sources: Acts of Peter, ch. 35, tr. M. R. James
Wikipedia, 'Church of Domine Quo Vadis' (Santa Maria in Palmis)
suggested_refs: The footprint slab at Santa Maria in Palmis, Via Appia Antica 51
Henryk Sienkiewicz, Quo Vadis (1896), which took its title from this scene

stops.name: The Circus of Nero, head downward
stops.date_confidence: The martyrdom at Rome under Nero is attested at Eusebius, Church History 2.25, written about 250 years after the event and supplying no year, no day, and no order relative to Paul; the conventional range is 64-68 and 66 here is a midpoint, not a finding. The inverted posture is R: it appears first in the Acts of Peter, late second century, and is repeated by Origen at Eusebius 3.1, while Tertullian, earlier, says only that Peter's passion was like his Lord's. The circus location comes from the Acts of Peter.
stops.campa: Between the turning posts of Nero's circus on the Vatican side of the river, in the gardens where the emperor burned Christians to light his evenings, they set up the cross. He asks the executioners to fix him to it the other way up, head toward the ground, because he does not judge himself worthy to die in the posture his Lord died in. The obelisk that stood on the spine of that circus is standing yet. It was dragged a few hundred yards in 1586 into the middle of the square that carries his name.
stops.quote: I beseech you the executioners, crucify me thus, with the head downward and not otherwise.
stops.quote_source: Acts of Peter, ch. 37, tr. M. R. James
sources: Origen, quoted at Eusebius, Church History 3.1
suggested_refs: The Vatican obelisk, moved by Domenico Fontana in 1586
Caravaggio, Crucifixion of Saint Peter, 1601, Cerasi Chapel, Santa Maria del Popolo

stops.name: Rome, the letter to the dispersion
stops.date_confidence: 1 Peter 1:1 and 5:12-13 are attested text; the authorship is not. Direct Petrine authorship is contested, and many critical scholars regard the letter as a Petrine-school or posthumous pseudonymous composition of c. 70-100, which is the range this date sits inside; the stop is placed after the martyrdom for that reason, and the placement is an argument, not a neutral ordering. The reading of Babylon as a cipher for Rome is standard but itself disputed, and the pin follows that reading.
stops.campa: A letter goes out to exiles scattered across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, five provinces of northern Asia Minor, telling them to hold steady under suffering and to have an answer ready for anyone who asks about their hope. It is written, it says, through Silvanus, and it closes with greetings from the church in Babylon and from my son Mark. Babylon by then is rubble and has been for centuries. The city that took Jerusalem apart is the one every reader is meant to think of.
stops.quote: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To the exiles of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.
suggested_refs: The five provinces of 1 Peter 1:1, the same regions Origen later assigns to Peter's preaching

segments.name: The Trophy on the Vatican Hill

stops.name: Rome, the letter that says only that he suffered
stops.date_confidence: 1 Clement 5-6, conventionally dated about 96 and written from the Roman church to Corinth. It is the earliest post-New Testament witness to Peter's death and is notably vague: it names no city and no manner of death. The Lightfoot text as printed at earlychristianwritings.com is corrupted at a line break, duplicating not one where the Greek has not one nor two; the Roberts-Donaldson rendering is quoted here instead. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: A generation after the fire, the church at Rome writes to the church at Corinth about jealousy and what it costs, and reaches for examples close at hand. It names Peter, who endured many labors and then bore his witness and went to the place of glory owed him, and then Paul, who wore chains seven times, was driven out and stoned, and reached the limits of the west. Around the two of them the letter sets a great multitude of the elect who suffered with them. That is all of it. No city, no cross, no circus, no year.
stops.quote: Peter, through unrighteous envy, endured not one or two, but numerous labours; and when he had at length suffered martyrdom, departed to the place of glory due to him.
sources: 1 Clement 5:4, Lightfoot, at earlychristianwritings.com, corrupt at the line break
suggested_refs: 1 Clement, the earliest surviving Christian letter outside the New Testament

stops.name: Vatican Hill, the trophies Gaius points to
stops.date_confidence: Gaius of Rome, quoted at Eusebius, Church History 2.25.7, written about 200 and preserved in the early fourth century. This is the earliest surviving text pointing to a specific Roman burial site for Peter. It attests an established local memorial tradition by that date; it identifies no remains and proves nothing forensic. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: A Roman presbyter named Gaius is arguing with a Montanist called Proclus, who has been boasting about the tombs of Philip's daughters in Asia. Gaius answers with what his own city can show. Go to the Vatican, he says, or go out along the road to Ostia, and you will find the trophies of the men who laid the foundations of this church. There is no basilica on that hill yet, and will not be for another century. What he points at are two markers a man could walk out to on an afternoon, and he expects his opponent to know they are there.
stops.quote: But I can show the trophies of the apostles. For if you will go to the Vatican or to the Ostian way, you will find the trophies of those who laid the foundations of this church.
stops.quote_source: Gaius of Rome, quoted in Eusebius, Church History 2.25
suggested_refs: The second-century aedicula against the Red Wall, the likely trophy Gaius means

stops.name: The catacombs on the Appian Way, in catacumbas
stops.date_confidence: R. Third-century liturgical calendars, the Depositio Martyrum and the Martyrologium Hieronymianum, record the apostles' memory in catacumbas at this site, conventionally under the year 258, which is the date used here. Whether relics of Peter and Paul were actually moved here and later returned, and why, remains debated among archaeologists.
stops.campa: Three miles out on the Appian Way, in a hollow the Romans called ad catacumbas, a walled courtyard fills with scratched invocations to Peter and to Paul, hundreds of them, cut by people who came out to eat funeral meals in the open air. The old calendars mark the twenty-ninth of June at this address. Some archaeologists read the graffiti as proof the bones were brought here for safekeeping in a persecution and taken back afterward. Others read the same walls as a memorial that never held a body.
sources: Depositio Martyrum and Martyrologium Hieronymianum, as summarized there
suggested_refs: The triclia graffiti wall under San Sebastiano fuori le mura
The joint feast of Peter and Paul, 29 June, in both Western and Eastern calendars

stops.name: Vatican Hill, Constantine builds over the grave
stops.date_confidence: Construction of Old St Peter's began between 318 and 322 and took about forty years; 320 is a midpoint within that bracket. The engineering itself is the evidence: the site sloped hard over a working pagan necropolis and demanded enormous substructures, which is strong evidence that fourth-century Christians would not consider moving the spot. It says nothing about whose bones lay under it. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The emperor puts his basilica on the worst possible ground in Rome for a basilica. The hill slopes off sharply, the site is a crowded pagan cemetery still taking burials, and to get a level floor the engineers have to fill and buttress and bury whole mausoleums with their painted walls and their inscriptions intact. Forty years of that labor buys one thing: an altar standing directly over a small second-century shrine of two colonnettes and a slab, set against a wall painted red.
sources: Toynbee and Ward Perkins, The Shrine of St Peter and the Vatican Excavations (1956)
suggested_refs: The buried mausoleums of the Vatican necropolis, sealed by Constantine's fill

stops.name: San Pietro in Vincoli, the two chains fused
stops.date_confidence: The church's consecration in 439 under Sixtus III is attested. The chain of custody is traditional and the fusion legend is R. The research pool's Empress Eudoxia giving Jerusalem chains to Leo I in 438-439 conflates two women and mis-dates the gift: Aelia Eudocia obtained the chains at Jerusalem from Juvenal, probably 438-439, and her daughter Licinia Eudoxia, wife of Valentinian III, presented them to Pope Leo I, who reigned from 440. Corrected here. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: An empress on pilgrimage in Jerusalem is given the chains that held Peter in Herod's prison and sends them west. Her daughter puts them into the hands of the pope at Rome. He holds them up against the other chains, the ones from the last imprisonment in this city, and the two lengths of iron close on each other and become a single chain that cannot be taken apart again. A basilica goes up on the Esquiline to keep them. They lie there now in a bronze and glass case beneath the main altar.
suggested_refs: The reliquary of the chains under the high altar of San Pietro in Vincoli
The skull relic claimed for Peter at the Archbasilica of St John Lateran, attested from at least the ninth century

stops.name: The Vatican necropolis, the shrine under the altar
stops.date_confidence: The necropolis was rediscovered in 1939, while a tomb was being cut for Pius XI, and excavated under Ludwig Kaas through 1949; the research pool's 1940-1949 is corrected to 1939, which its own afterlife lens already gave. What was found is attested. What it means is not. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Workmen cutting a grave for a dead pope in the crypt break through into a street of Roman tombs, roofed and stuccoed and packed with the ordinary dead of the second century, running the length of the basilica above them. Ten years of excavation follow that street west and uphill until it ends directly beneath the high altar at a small niche of two colonnettes and a slab, set against a wall painted red and covered over with graffiti. It is the shrine Constantine laid his floor around, unseen for sixteen centuries.
sources: Toynbee and Ward Perkins, The Shrine of St Peter and the Vatican Excavations (1956)
suggested_refs: The Red Wall and the graffiti wall of the Vatican necropolis
The scavi beneath St Peter's, opened to guided visits

stops.name: Vatican City, the announcement of the bones
stops.date_confidence: The announcement of 26 June 1968 is an attested event; the identification it announced is disputed and remains R. Bones were removed from a niche in the graffiti wall by Ludwig Kaas in 1942 without archaeological documentation. Venerando Correnti of Palermo examined them in 1962 and concluded they belonged to a robust man of about sixty to seventy. Margherita Guarducci, an epigrapher, built the Petrine identification on top of that finding; the research pool's attribution of the osteology to Guarducci is corrected here. Antonio Ferrua, who led the excavation, said publicly that he was not convinced.
stops.campa: The bones had been taken out of a niche in the graffiti wall in 1942, without a record, and set aside in a storeroom for twenty years. An anatomist then reads them as one man, heavily built, sixty to seventy years old. An epigrapher reads the scratched Greek beside the niche as saying that Peter is here. On the twenty-sixth of June the pope announces that the relics have been identified in a manner he believes convincing. The archaeologist who ran the dig for nine years says in public that he is not convinced.
sources: Zander, The Necropolis under St Peter's Basilica, on the Guarducci and Ferrua dispute
suggested_refs: Margherita Guarducci's reading of the graffiti-wall inscriptions
Antonio Ferrua's published objections to the excavation sequence

stops.name: St Peter's, the bones brought out
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Nine bone fragments were displayed publicly for the first time at the closing Mass of the Year of Faith, 24 November 2013. The display is an event and settles no question about whose bones they are; the identification stands where 1968 left it.
stops.campa: On the last Sunday of the Year of Faith they carry the fragments out into the open in a bronze case and set them on the altar steps in front of the crowd, and a pope holds the case for a while during the Mass. Nine pieces of bone, and no one has ever settled whether they are his. The square stands on the circus, the basilica stands on the necropolis, and the necropolis stands on a hillside that lay outside the city walls when a fisherman from the Sea of Galilee was killed on it.
suggested_refs: The bronze reliquary of the nine fragments, displayed 24 November 2013
Michelangelo Buonarroti's Pieta and the dome of St Peter's, raised over the same grave in 1498-1564
